transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-18
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~56 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marco Diaz (Redwood SE), Priya Sharma (Redwood SRE), Ethan Morales (Perf Eng), Olivia Chen (BlueVector ML), Samir Gupta (BlueVector Infra), Priya Desai (BlueVector Security), Noah Brown (BlueVector Product)
Links referenced: Deck - https://redwood.example.com/decks/moe-routing-runtime.pdf, Bench spreadsheet - https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/bv-moe-bench.xlsx, Security pack - https://redwood.example.com/security/soc2.pdf

Summary (auto-gen): Discussed MoE routing overheads per-token and strategies to reduce effective cost (top-k gating, router offload, token batching). Covered rope/rotary scaling artifacts with very long contexts and mitigation via prefix chunking and KV eviction. Quantization impacts on model accuracy vs throughput were debated; recommended mixed approaches depending on workload.

00:00:05 - Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick intro, Marco and Priya from our side are gonna go deep on routing costs and perf. Olivia / Samir, feel free to jump in with your perf numbers, right?
00:00:18 - Olivia Chen: Yeah thanks Lena, hi all. We run a real-time summarization pipeline, 8k windows, occasional 32k full docs. Latency target is 300 ms p95 for single-turn, avg throughput about 120 reqs/min. We're exploring MoE to keep model quality without full large dense model costs.
00:00:34 - Marco Diaz: Got it - so the two main things we need to compare are the per-token route overhead (router compute + cross-device dispatch) and the sparse expert inference actual compute. In many setups the router can dominate at short seqs if not optimized.
00:00:52 - Samir Gupta: Can you clarify router costs? Is it just a small MLP per token? How does it scale with experts (say 64 experts)?
00:01:05 - Marco Diaz: Yeah so router is an MLP gating function. For top-1 routing it's cheap-ish but you still have a softmax and potentially load-balancing losses; top-2 doubles the routing decisions and the memory movement. With 64 experts the dispatch metadata and scatter/gather overhead becomes nontrivial esp across GPUs. If experts are on different devices you pay host/device transfers unless you colocate.
00:01:28 - Priya Desai: From a security angle, cross-GPU dispatch inside a VPC is ok, but we want audit logs for what tokens went to which expert for compliance reasons. Is that feasible?
:01:37 - Priya Sharma: Uh yeah we can enable trace logging at the router layer; it's a perf tradeoff though. The logging adds 5-15% extra latency if you write per-token traces; better to sample or log aggregated metrics per batch.

00:02:05 - Ethan Morales: I also want to flag Kv cache interactions: when you have MoE + KV cache, your cache hit patterns can change because experts specialize and keys/values might be sharded. If KV is sharded by expert, lookups can cross devices. Two mitigations: a) maintain a thin local KV cache of recent prefixes, b) route cache lookups through a unified host-resident cache that minimizes GPU-to-GPU hops.
00:02:38 - Olivia Chen: We currently do unified cache on host but it's adding 40-60ms at tail. Would a local GPU-resident prefix cache help?
00:02:49 - Marco Diaz: Yes for tail latency local GPU KV is best; you need to budget VRAM. For example a 16k context prefix cache for one stream at float16 keys could be tens of MBs per stream. If you pin experts and keep their KV local you reduce hops.

00:03:30 - Noah Brown: Quick clarifying q: when you say "pin experts" do you mean static placement or dynamic hot-swap?
00:03:37 - Marco Diaz: Pinning means static placement per expert to a GPU to avoid cross-host transfer. Dynamic placement can be done but then you need a scheduler that migrates KV. For most production it's simpler to pin a balanced partition.

00:04:10 - Samir Gupta: How does rope/rotary scaling come into play? We saw drifting attention weights with 32k context on Mistral-like models.
00:04:20 - Marco Diaz: Good question. There are two common issues: absolute positional embeddings (rope/rotary) that weren't trained for extreme lengths can cause aliasing. Also internal chunking or kv-indexing mistakes can lead to off-by-one offsets and then attention looks weird. Strategy: chunk long context into overlapping windows, use relative position bias patches, and where possible apply extrapolation factors that some forks of Llama/Mistral support. We also suggest running a short calibration sweep: feed synthetic long sequences to measure attention drift.
00:05:02 - Olivia Chen: We did a calibration and saw quality drop after ~12k for Llama-deriv. For Mistral it was worse. Any quantization-specific behavior here?
00:05:12 - Marco Diaz: Quantization can amplify noise in attention scores so yes you may see earlier degradation. 8-bit often is safe, 4-bit needs careful per-layer scaling (PTQ vs QAT). Our runtime supports group-wise quant scales and per-channel for attention matrices which helps.

00:05:50 - Lena Park: Can we get concrete numbers? Marco, do you have sample bench numbers for top-1 vs top-2 routing, and for 8-bit vs 4-bit quant?
00:06:00 - Marco Diaz: Yep quick gist from bench: baseline dense Llama-3 13B float16: 1-token latency (batch=1) ~ 120 ms. MoE variant (13B with 16 experts) top-1 routing optimized, colocation of experts: 130-160 ms depending on dispatch. Top-2 routing adds ~30-60% latency for small batches because of duplicate token compute. 8-bit quant for experts saves 20-30% latency on kernels, 4-bit (well tuned) saves up to 40-50% but with a small hit to generation quality unless you use per-channel/scaling. These are rough but we have spreadsheet to share.
00:06:45 - Samir Gupta: If top-1 only is better latency-wise, is there quality regression vs top-2?
00:06:55 - Marco Diaz: In many tasks top-1 is competitive if experts are sufficiently specialized and trained with router top-1. Top-2 helps with redundancy and smoothing. For summarization task it's often marginal improvement; for instruction-fusion tasks it's bigger. So it depends on your eval set.

00:07:30 - Priya Desai: On VPC/on-prem: what's the simplest config to preserve low latency? You're suggesting Dedicated with colocated experts?
00:07:42 - Ethan Morales: For shortest path: Dedicated (single-tenant) cluster with NVLink-enabled GPUs and colocated experts + local NVMe-backed KV resident caches. That avoids host hops and keeps p95 low. For on-prem you need an RDMA fabric and careful NUMA tuning.

00:08:10 - Olivia Chen: Our infra constraints: limited NVLink, mostly single GPU per node with 80GB A10gs and limited rack-level NVLink. How much worse would cross-node MoE be?
00:08:24 - Marco Diaz: Cross-node incurs network hop latency and serialization overhead; if you can't NVLink, you should minimize cross-node dispatch. Options: reduce number of experts and make them wider (fewer experts larger capacity), or deploy a hybrid where the router does a cheap heuristic to route to local experts and fallback to remote only on misses.
00:08:52 - Lena Park: Also consider using model surgery: convert some MoE layers to dense in inference to reduce routing cost while keeping training MoE. That reduces routing overhead and may be a good tradeoff.

00:09:20 - Samir Gupta: About batching: you mentioned continuous batching earlier. For our traffic (spiky), what's recommended?
00:09:28 - Marco Diaz: Continuous batching with adaptive max-wait (tunable ms window) is ideal. For spiky traffic, we use small max-wait (~15ms) to keep latency target; for background bulk, increase window. Also we dynamically adjust batch composition for MoE so tokens that route to same expert are processed together—this improves GPU utilization but requires a router-aware batcher.
00:09:58 - Olivia Chen: That router-aware batching sounds complex — does Redwood runtime support it out of the box?
00:10:05 - Marco Diaz: Yes our runtime supports continuous batching + router-aware grouping and can fall back to naive batching. We provided a sample config in the deck.

00:11:00 - Noah Brown: Any notes on warmup / KV eviction policies? We want predictable p95.
00:11:07 - Priya Sharma: Warmup: keep a small pool of hot contexts resident; eviction policy should be time-based with LRU windows, but for MoE consider expert locality — evict keys that belong to low-activity experts first. Also pre-warm on expected queries when possible.

00:11:45 - Olivia Chen: What about evals? How should we compare dense vs MoE properly?
00:11:51 - Marco Diaz: Evaluate on lat/throughput + quality delta at the same latency budget. Use a fixed p95 SLA (e.g., 300ms) and measure tokens/sec and ROUGE/BLEU/ROSTER whatever. Also compare cost-per-token including routing overhead and ingress/egress. We can help run those evals.

00:12:20 - Samir Gupta: Security question: how granular are the audit logs and can we mask tokens?
00:12:29 - Priya Sharma: We can mask sensitive tokens at the tokenizer layer before logging and still capture routing metadata (which expert handled which token) as anonymized IDs. Full plaintext logging is optional and discouraged for PII.

00:13:05 - Marco Diaz: Small gotcha on quantization: some kernel libraries (custom fused kernels) don't support 4-bit for all ops, particularly some attention math; fallback paths incur overhead. We typically recommend testing the exact kernel stack on your GPU type.
00:13:30 - Olivia Chen: We're using A10gs — any known regressions?
00:13:35 - Marco Diaz: A10 family is fine for 8-bit and many 4-bit kernels but NVidia driver/kernel combos matter. We'll include driver recommendations in the bench sheet.

00:14:20 - Lena Park: Let's look at the bench sheet briefly (Marco shares).
00:14:25 - (screen share / unsaid)
00:15:20 - Marco Diaz: Here are a few concrete rows: Llama-13B dense float16 batch1 - 120ms; Llama-13B MoE-16 top1 colocated - 150ms; MoE-16 top2 colocated - 210ms; MoE-16 top1 cross-node - 210ms; MoE-16 top1 colocated + 4-bit experts - 90ms. Note that the 4-bit optimized kernels yielded the biggest speedups when they hit the fast path.
00:16:05 - Samir Gupta: That 90ms number seems almost too good — is quality acceptable?
00:16:11 - Marco Diaz: 4-bit with per-channel scale + small calibration dataset gave <1.5% delta on our summarization metric for that model. But you'd want to validate on your eval set.

00:16:45 - Olivia Chen: On rope scaling again: you implied adapter patches exist. Is that stable?
00:16:52 - Marco Diaz: There are a few community patches that extend rotary/rope extrapolation; some are stable enough for inference but they change logits slightly; again we recommend a calibration run. Redwood can run a quick sweep for you.

00:17:30 - Noah Brown: Any recommendations for hybrid routing (top-1 mostly with occasional top-2)?
00:17:37 - Marco Diaz: Yes a heuristic: route top-1 by default, but if router confidence < threshold then compute top-2 for that token. That saves compute for most tokens and adds redundancy where router is uncertain. It adds complexity but is often the right balance.

00:18:20 - Priya Desai: From compliance: does Redwood redact logs in the control plane for hosted?
00:18:26 - Lena Park: We offer options: redact at the edge, token-level masking, or encrypted-at-rest with access controls. We'll share the security pack.

00:18:58 - Marco Diaz: A few operational recommendations: 1) measure per-expert load distribution continuously, 2) set autoscale policies keyed on router queue depth and expert GPU utilization, 3) use fallback dense model route for backoff if experts are overloaded.

00:19:30 - Olivia Chen: Autoscaling onto more GPUs — is cold-start an issue for KV caches?
00:19:37 - Marco Diaz: Yes cold-start is expensive; cache warmup can take seconds to minutes. Use rolling scale and pre-warm nodes based on forecasted traffic.

00:20:00 - Samir Gupta: Any recommended guardrails in the runtime config we should start with?
00:20:06 - Marco Diaz: We usually recommend: max-wait 15ms, max-batch 32 for low-latency; router-confidence threshold 0.7 for top-1; per-expert max-token cap to avoid hot experts; and kv local cache size set to hold your most recent 50 tokens per stream.

00:21:00 - (table-specific discussion, minor interruptions)
00:30:05 - Olivia Chen: Real-world worry: our logs show uneven expert load despite balanced training. Could tokenization or prompt style be skewing?
00:30:14 - Marco Diaz: Absolutely — tokenization artifacts and prompt engineering cause skew. Quick fixes: normalize prompts, add temperature to router loss during fine-tune, or use auxiliary load-balancing loss.

00:35:00 - Priya Desai: For on-prem we need to confirm encryption at rest for KV and key management; does Redwood support HSM/KMS integration?
00:35:10 - Priya Sharma: Yes Redwood Private supports KMS/HSM integrations and customer-managed keys; we can surface the exact connectors.

00:40:20 - Lena Park: Time check - 15 minutes left - any remaining deep topics?
00:40:27 - Samir Gupta: One more: what's the recommended quant pipeline for production? PTQ or QAT?
00:40:35 - Marco Diaz: Start with PTQ per-channel with calibration dataset. If you need tighter quality, use QAT during a short finetune or LoRA-style quant-aware finetune. For MoE experts you can mix: quantize stable experts aggressively and leave sensitive experts in higher precision.

00:42:00 - Olivia Chen: Is there an easy way to simulate cost-per-token with routing overheads included?
00:42:08 - Marco Diaz: Yes our benchmark spreadsheet models per-token router op, expert op, cross-node transfer, and amortized KV cost. We'll share the spreadsheet and can plug in your traffic shape.

00:44:30 - Lena Park: Alright last block - recap of actions and timeline. Marco can you bullet next week bench deliverable?
00:44:38 - Marco Diaz: Deliverable: per-model rows for Llama-13B, Mistral-7B, Qwen-14B; modes: dense, MoE top-1/2, quant 8/4 bit; batch sizes 1/4/16; metrics: p50/p95 latency, throughput, cost-per-token. Target 2025-06-23.
00:45:05 - Olivia Chen: Great. Also can we get an initial pilot contract for Dedicated with limited 3-month commit? Samir will coordinate.
00:45:16 - Lena Park: We'll get a contract draft after the bench.

00:46:00 - (closing remarks)
00:46:10 - Lena Park: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the sheet and SOC2.
00:46:20 - Noah Brown: Thanks all.
00:46:25 - Samir Gupta: Appreciate it, talk soon.

End transcript.
